newsitem.title: USA: Little sympathy in town for California suicides.
newsitem.headline: Little sympathy in town for California suicides.

text.p: The 39 people who apparently committed mass suicide in a luxury mansion in this exclusive neighbourhood got little sympathy on Thursday from people who live and work here.
"There's a lot of weirdos in Rancho Santa Fe," said Zal Derkach, who works in a radio and TV appliance store in the affluent suburb of San Diego.

"There are all sorts of loons in this world and I am not shocked. I grew up with the Jim Jones thing," he said, referring to the 1978 Jonestown, Guyana, mass suicide in which more than 900 people died.
On Wednesday, the bodies of 39 men and women were found in a $1.6 million hillside mansion at 18241 Colina Norte. Police believe they killed themselves with overdoses of drugs.

Set in rolling hills of eucalyptus and citrus trees, the unincorporated area was formed under a "covenant" in 1928 and is the oldest planned community in California. Rancho Santa Fe is so named because it was formed by the Santa Fe Railroad.

Some 20 miles (32 km) north of San Diego, Rancho Santa Fe is considered the second most expensive zip code in California after Beverly Hills. The median home price is $1.4 million, and the minimum size of a building plot is 2.86 acres (1.157 hectares).
The town's residents have the highest median income in San Diego County -- $93,000 a year.
Known to residents simply as The Ranch, many of the homes have neatly fenced horse pastures. Over the years, The Ranch has been home to the rich and famous.

Actors Douglas Fairbanks, Mary Pickford and Robert Young called it home, as did astronaut Wally Schirra. It is still home to author Joseph Wambaugh ("The Onion Field") and San Diego Padres owner John Moores. Pop singer Jewel recently bought an estate here.

On Thursday, some residents were shocked by the grisly find: "Nothing like this has ever happened here before," contractor Ron Rimmer said. And Jim Soucy, manager of the local 7-11 convenience store, said: "It makes you wonder what other things go on behind locked mansion gates."
Two teenage girls said they skipped school in nearby San Marcos to come and gawk, although the public was kept more than half a mile (0.8 km) away from the mansion.
"Why didn't they just live and raise babies instead of killing themselves?" asked Lindsey Nerheim, 16. "It's whacked. Why would all those people be dumb like that?"
Her friend, Nicole Pearce, surveying dozens of reporters and TV crews swarming around, snapped, "They're making too big a deal out of it."

Larry Purdue, a road worker with San Diego County, said he could hardly believe that such a thing could happen in a town full of Rolls-Royces, Mercedes and Jaguars where "people are riding horses and it's mellow.
"People out here are isolated in their homes -- they don't know their neighbours. In a way, it's not going to affect anything -- it just happened in that home, it wasn't the people of the town."
"It was a bunch of crazies that committed suicide," Purdue said.
Marilyn Van Slyke, a landscaper in town for 23 years, also stressed that the suicides were "not people of our community.
"To be honest, if they felt they needed to go on to their next life, so be it. If they can't deal with what's happening in the world right now ... they made their choice."
Becky Thompson, who runs an aquatic business in town, said, "I have never seen anything like this in my whole life -- at least not in the United States. And we're walking around with these people?"
One vacationing family of four from Chicago changed its itinerary on Thursday to include Rancho Santa Fe.
"We were going to the zoo today, but ended up here," said Jill Kooken, explaining that her 11-year-old daughter wanted to be a TV reporter.
